title: Offshore Renewable-Energy Systems
analyses: Tidal turbine hydrodynamic and performance analysis
Offshore wind turbine aerodynamic loading analysis

scope: Applicable to fixed and floating offshore wind, tidal-stream turbines, wave-energy converters, floating solar installations and other offshore renewable systems.

models.text: The suite should implement conservation of mass, momentum and energy, Navier–Stokes equations, Euler equations, Bernoulli's equation, blade element momentum theory, actuator-disc momentum theory, actuator-line theory, Prandtl tip-loss corrections, Glauert high-thrust corrections, dynamic inflow models, Beddoes–Leishman dynamic stall, lifting-line theory and vortex lattice methods.

The suite should include Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations, Spalart–Allmaras turbulence modelling, k–epsilon models, k–omega SST models, Reynolds stress models, large-eddy simulation, detached-eddy simulation, wall functions, near-wall treatment models and aeroelastic fluid–structure interaction.

The suite should employ Airy wave theory, Stokes higher-order wave theory, wave spectra, Morison's equation, potential-flow diffraction and radiation theory, boundary-element hydrodynamics, nonlinear free-surface models, shallow-water equations, tidal current momentum equations, turbulence modelling, actuator-disc hydrodynamics and blade element momentum models adapted to tidal turbines.

The suite should implement linear wave radiation and diffraction, Cummins' impulse response equation, hydrodynamic added mass and radiation damping, nonlinear Froude–Krylov loading, power-take-off force models, hydraulic PTO dynamics, generator electromechanical models, latching control, reactive control and optimal energy absorption formulations.

The suite should incorporate Euler–Bernoulli beam theory, Timoshenko beam theory, geometrically exact beam models, composite laminate theory, finite-element structural dynamics, modal analysis, coupled rotor–tower–foundation dynamics, nonlinear material constitutive models, fatigue damage, rainflow counting and fracture mechanics.

models.group: Foundation, floating platform and mooring models
models.text: The suite should include nonlinear pile–soil resistance, foundation bearing capacity, suction bucket mechanics, offshore structural stability, six-degree-of-freedom floating-body dynamics, hydrostatic restoring, catenary mooring equations, dynamic mooring models, anchor holding capacity and seabed scour modelling.

The suite should implement Faraday's electromagnetic induction law, Maxwell's equations, electrical machine d–q axis models, permanent magnet synchronous generator models, induction generator models, electromagnetic torque relationships, power electronic switching models, averaged converter models, AC/DC conversion, transformer models, electrical power flow, cable resistance and thermal loss models.

The suite should include turbine power coefficient models, tip-speed ratio formulations, Betz limit theory, generator torque control, blade pitch control, maximum power point tracking, proportional–integral–derivative control, state-space control, model predictive control, Kalman filtering, fault detection and supervisory control.

The suite should include Jensen/Park wake models, Gaussian wake deficit models, Bastankhah–Porté-Agel wake formulations, Frandsen turbulence models, wake superposition, dynamic wake meandering, actuator-line CFD wake prediction, turbine blockage models and array-level energy optimization.

models.group: Floating solar and energy performance models
models.text: The suite should employ photovoltaic single-diode and double-diode equivalent circuit models, irradiance transposition models, solar cell temperature models, photovoltaic thermal derating, solar array electrical network models, buoyancy stability, floating platform wave-response models and combined solar–hydrodynamic interaction.

The suite should support fully coupled aero-hydro-servo-elastic simulation, rotor CFD–structural finite-element coupling, wind resource–wake–power production integration, hydro-electromechanical wave-energy conversion, floating wind turbine–mooring–cable interaction, stochastic environmental simulation, probabilistic reliability and physics-based digital twins. Machine-learning-assisted wake prediction and surrogate optimization may be added when validated against the relevant physical models and datasets.

subtitle: Fixed/floating offshore wind, tidal-stream turbines, wave-energy converters, floating solar, power-take-off systems and array performance.
ic: The initial conditions shall establish the installed geometry and operating state of the renewable-energy device, including the turbine rotor, blades, tower, foundation, floating platform, power-take-off system and associated mooring or support structures.

For offshore wind systems, the initial turbine state shall include rotor speed, blade pitch, yaw orientation, generator torque, structural deflections and control-system operating state. For tidal turbines, the initial conditions shall establish rotor speed, blade orientation, current field and generator state.

For wave-energy converters, the initial state shall define the floating or submerged body position, velocity, orientation, hydrostatic equilibrium and power-take-off settings. Mooring tensions and initial platform displacement shall be consistent with the starting environmental conditions.

The fluid environment shall have specified initial wind velocity, water velocity, wave elevation and turbulence conditions according to the modelling approach. Structural fatigue analysis shall include accumulated fatigue damage where relevant.

For floating solar systems, the initial state shall define platform buoyancy, orientation, mooring equilibrium, panel operating temperature, initial solar irradiance and electrical operating conditions.

Array simulations shall initialize turbine or device operating states and the relevant inflow or wake field. Energy-production simulations shall begin with a defined resource and operational availability state.
bc: Wind turbine aerodynamic boundaries shall prescribe incoming wind velocity, turbulence, wind shear and directional conditions, together with appropriate far-field and wake-outflow treatments.

Tidal turbine boundaries shall impose water-current inflow, downstream outflow, appropriate seabed and free-surface conditions, and lateral domain conditions that do not unrealistically constrain the flow.

Wave-energy converter boundaries shall prescribe incident wave conditions, free-surface behaviour, wave radiation and power-take-off mechanical loading. Floating-device boundaries shall include mooring reactions, hydrostatic support and hydrodynamic loading.

At the foundation, boundaries shall represent pile–soil interaction, gravity-foundation contact or other appropriate seabed restraints. Structural interfaces shall preserve load and displacement continuity between blades, hub, shaft, nacelle, tower and foundation.

Control-system boundaries shall prescribe generator torque limits, blade pitch limits, yaw-control behaviour, braking conditions and startup/shutdown rules. Electrical boundaries shall represent generator connections, converters, transformers and the receiving electrical network.

For floating solar systems, structural boundaries shall account for buoyancy, wave loading, mooring restraint and thermal exchange with the surrounding environment. Solar-energy conversion shall use prescribed irradiance, ambient temperature and applicable electrical operating constraints.

For array simulations, inflow conditions, turbine spacing and wake interactions shall be specified. Energy-production simulations shall use the appropriate time-varying resource conditions and availability constraints.

calibration: Calibration should use wind tunnel testing, tidal turbine experiments, wave-energy converter basin tests, floating platform experiments, manufacturer qualification testing and measured renewable-energy system operating data.

Offshore wind turbine aerodynamic parameters should be calibrated using wind tunnel measurements, blade aerodynamic tests, rotor performance measurements and supervisory control and data acquisition records. Turbine thrust, torque, power output and operating response should be considered across a representative range of wind speeds.

Blade structural stiffness, damping and fatigue parameters should be calibrated against composite material testing, static blade loading experiments, modal measurements and full-scale blade fatigue tests.
Integrated turbine control parameters should be calibrated using measured pitch response, generator torque, rotor speed and operational control behaviour.
Tidal turbine models should be calibrated using measured water velocities, rotor torque, turbine thrust, power production and hydrodynamic loading from laboratory or field experiments.

Wave-energy converter models should use wave-basin measurements of body motion, wave excitation, damping, restoring characteristics and absorbed power. Power-take-off damping and conversion parameters should be informed by equipment performance testing.
Floating renewable platform models should be calibrated using hydrostatic tests, motion decay experiments, mooring measurements and representative coupled system experiments.
Wake interaction models should be calibrated using wind farm operational data, lidar measurements, turbine-to-turbine power variation and representative wake experiments.
Scour models should be calibrated using seabed surveys, sediment measurements and physical experiments.
Electrical conversion and transmission models should use generator tests, converter efficiency measurements, cable thermal measurements and certified electrical equipment characteristics.
Floating solar models should use measured solar irradiance, module temperature, photovoltaic output, platform motion and environmental exposure data.
verification: Aerodynamic calculations should be verified against established blade and rotor benchmark problems, prescribed inflow cases and independently calculated reference solutions.
Hydrodynamic models should undergo wave and current benchmark comparisons, spatial convergence studies and temporal convergence tests.
Structural calculations should be verified against beam, shell, composite laminate, foundation and fatigue benchmark problems.

Integrated aero-hydro-servo-elastic simulations should undergo component-level verification before full-system coupling. Load transfer, control signals, rotor dynamics, platform motion and foundation reactions should be checked for consistency.
Control-system implementations should be tested against prescribed operating sequences, startup conditions, shutdown events and fault-response cases.
Wave-energy converter calculations should be checked against known floating-body response benchmarks and independently calculated power-take-off reference cases.
Tidal turbine power and thrust calculations should undergo mesh convergence, rotational discretization and time-step sensitivity studies where CFD or transient rotor calculations are used.
Electrical power calculations should be checked against prescribed generator, converter, transformer and cable reference cases.
Wake calculations should undergo spatial resolution and array-layout sensitivity testing.
Annual energy production calculations should be verified using independently calculated energy aggregation and loss-accounting benchmarks.
Reliability calculations should be tested using known failure distributions and reproducible probabilistic sampling.
validation: Offshore wind aerodynamic loading, rotor speed, power production and blade response should be compared against independent wind tunnel experiments, turbine field measurements and operational monitoring records.
Integrated structural response should be evaluated using measured turbine accelerations, tower strains, blade loads and foundation behaviour.
Tidal turbine thrust, torque and electrical power predictions should be validated using independent laboratory or field turbine measurements.
Wave-energy converter motions, absorbed power and power-take-off behaviour should be assessed using independent wave-basin experiments or instrumented demonstrations.
Floating platform motions and mooring loads should be compared with basin tests and offshore demonstration measurements.
Wake and array performance predictions should be evaluated using wind farm or tidal array operating measurements that were not used for calibration.

Annual energy production predictions should be compared with independent production records over representative operating periods, while accounting for availability, curtailment and environmental variability.
Electrical system losses and cable temperatures should be assessed using equipment testing and measured operating data.
Floating solar performance should be compared with independently measured module temperatures, irradiance and energy generation.
Component fatigue and lifetime predictions should be evaluated using qualification tests, inspection records, measured structural response and documented component failures.

geometry.text: Fixed offshore wind turbines, floating wind platforms, tidal-stream turbines, wave-energy converters, floating photovoltaic systems, support structures, foundations, mooring systems, subsea power cables and renewable-energy arrays.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS, IFC, DXF and supported DWG should be accepted for rotor blades, hubs, nacelles, towers, marine foundations, floating platforms, power-take-off components, generators, mechanical supports and floating solar assemblies.

geometry.cat: Aerodynamic rotor and blade geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, STL, OBJ, NURBS surfaces, DXF airfoil profiles, Selig-compatible airfoil coordinate files (.dat), CSV airfoil coordinate datasets, and documented XML/JSON blade-geometry descriptions should be supported. Blade geometries should preserve airfoil sections, spanwise station locations, chord distribution, twist distribution, leading and trailing edges, blade root geometry and blade surface continuity.

geometry.cat: Marine turbine and wave-energy geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, NURBS, STL, OBJ and hydrodynamic panel-mesh representations should be supported for tidal rotor blades, ducts, support structures, oscillating bodies, point absorbers, oscillating-water-column chambers and floating wave-energy devices. WAMIT-compatible GDF and supported NEMOH-style hydrodynamic mesh files should be accepted for appropriate potential-flow models.

IFC, SDNF, STEP, IGES, LandXML, GML, GeoTIFF, XYZ, LAS/LAZ and suitable pile/foundation structural models should be supported for floating platforms, mooring arrangements, wind turbine foundations, tidal foundation structures and seabed interaction.

geometry.cat: Computational aerodynamic, hydrodynamic and structural formats
geometry.text: CGNS, SU2, OpenFOAM polyMesh, Gmsh MSH, Nastran BDF/NAS, Abaqus INP, ANSYS CDB, MED, UNV, VTK/VTU and Exodus should be accepted for compatible aerodynamic meshes, water-flow meshes, blade structural meshes, foundation models and coupled engineering analyses.

geometry.cat: Array layout and geospatial geometry formats
geometry.text: CSV, XYZ, GeoJSON, GML, GeoPackage, Shapefile, DXF, LandXML, GeoTIFF and NetCDF should be supported for wind-turbine coordinates, tidal-device arrangements, wave-energy converter arrays, seabed bathymetry, export-cable routes and installation-site geometries.

STL, OBJ, PLY, GLB, 3MF, LAS/LAZ, E57, photogrammetric surface meshes and point-cloud datasets should be accepted for prototype blades, scanned rotor geometries, damaged foundations, complex wave-energy converter shapes and existing renewable-energy structures.
